articles.title: How many govt, security officials died in 2024 general elections? CRPF officer moves Delhi HC for EC data - ThePrint
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: A serving Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) officer has moved the Delhi High Court seeking disclosure of government personnel fatalities nationwide during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.
The elections which happened April to June 2024 reportedly resulted in many on duty government and security officials dying due to the heatwave.
On Wednesday, the Delhi High Court issued notices on the writ petition filed by Rahul Solanki, an Assistant Commandant, challenging an order by the Central Information Commission (CIC) that, according to Solanki, shielded the Election Commission of India (ECI) from providing centralised casualty records.
Currently posted with the G/87 Battalion at Imphal, Manipur, and having personally participated in election deployment across sensitive zones, Solanki argues that force personnel and citizens have a constitutional right under Article 19(1)(a) to know the full extent and causes of fatalities during electoral exercises.
Solanki highlights that under Article 324 of the Constitution and Sections 28A and 159 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, all election personnel operate under the direct superintendence, control, and discipline of the ECI.
Shifting the burden onto individual citizens to file dozens of separate RTIs across every state, he believes, ignores the central authority of the Election Commission and turns the Right to Information into an illusory process.
“The grievance of the petitioner is that once the respondent (CIC officer) acknowledged that the information was available with the Chief Electoral Officers of the States/UTs, it became mandatory upon them to transfer the RTI Application to the concerned authorities in accordance with Section 6(3) of the RTI Act instead of compelling the petitioner to file numerous separate RTI applications before each State/UT authority,” the petition reads.
He is represented by advocates Anshul Kumar and Manish Mishra.
2 years from RTI to CIC to court
The legal battle started on 27 July 2024, when Solanki filed a Right to Information (RTI) query with the ECI, asking for the total number of government employees who died while on election duty during the 2024 General Parliamentary Elections and the specific cause of death for each deceased employee.
On 2 August 2024, the ECI’s Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) stated that the information was not maintained centrally at Nirvachan Sadan but “may be available” with Chief Electoral Officers (CEOs) across States and Union Territories. However, the ECI refused to transfer the application under Section 6(3) of the RTI Act, asserting that it involved multiple public authorities.
Section 6(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, requires a public authority to transfer an RTI application to another appropriate authority within five days if the requested information is held by them or relates more closely to their functions.
Solanki’s subsequent appeals yielded no result. The ECI First Appellate Authority advised Solanki to file separate RTI applications before every state and UT CEO individually.
On 30 April 2026, Chief Information Commissioner Raj Kumar Goyal dismissed Solanki’s second appeal, ruling that requiring the ECI to gather or transfer queries across all state CEOs constituted an “unwarranted demand” and citing administrative burden precedents.
What the petition specifically asks for
In his plea before the Delhi High Court, Solanki lays out four concrete prayers to hold electoral authorities accountable.
First, a writ of certiorari (an order a higher court issues to a lower court or tribunal to send up the records of a case for review) to quash and set aside the Central Information Commission’s order of April 2026, as arbitrary and contrary to the scheme of the RTI Act.
Second, a writ of mandamus (court order that commands a government official, lower court, or public body to properly perform a mandatory legal duty) by the HC directing the ECI to transfer his original RTI application under Section 6(3) to all Chief Electoral Officers across states and Union Territories, with explicit directions for time-bound disclosure.
Third, a judicially binding legal declaration that Section 6(3) of the RTI Act permits transferring an application to multiple public authorities when information is decentralised, applying Section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, where singular terms include plural instances.
And last, a direction to the ECI to systematically compile, maintain, and proactively publish all casualty records of election duty personnel under its Section 4 statutory obligations.
The matter is now listed in December 2026.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)
